blocks.text: So far, MCP has been about a single agent talking to tools, files, or databases. But agents increasingly need to talk to other agents too, asking a specialist agent to handle a subtask, or splitting a big job across several cooperating agents.

It turns out MCP works just as well for this, an agent can expose itself as an MCP server, with tools that represent what it knows how to do. Another agent then calls those tools exactly like it would call any other tool.

This lesson covers what changes when the thing on the other end of a tool call is itself a reasoning agent, how messages get framed for that exchange, and what goes wrong when two agents try to make decisions at the same moment.
1. What Agent to Agent Communication Means Here

blocks.alt: What Agent to Agent Communication Means Here
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163862-722011262.png
Agent to agent communication means one AI agent asking another AI agent to do something, and getting a result back, using MCP as the shared transport in between.
Neither agent needs to know the other's internal framework, prompt, or model. They only need to agree on the MCP messages that pass between them.
That agreement is what makes it possible to swap out either agent later, upgrade a model, rewrite a prompt, or replace an entire agent, without breaking the other side of the conversation.
2. Turning Agent B Into an MCP Server

blocks.alt: Turning Agent B Into an MCP Server
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163863-767635959.png
To be callable this way, Agent B does not need any special agent-to-agent protocol. It simply runs as an ordinary MCP server, the same shape covered in earlier lessons.

Each tool that Agent B exposes stands in for one thing it knows how to do, summarize a document, plan a trip, check a codebase for bugs. Agent A never sees Agent B's prompt or reasoning steps, only the tool's name, description, and schema.

blocks.title: A useful way to picture it
blocks.content: Agent B is a black box from Agent A's point of view. Agent A hands over arguments through a tool call and waits for a result, the same way it would treat a weather API.

blocks.text: 2.1 What Agent A Actually Sees
From Agent A's side, calling Agent B looks exactly like calling any other MCP tool, a name, a schema, and a result. There is no visible sign that a whole second agent sits behind it.
2.2 Naming Tools for What They Do
Because Agent A only sees the tool's name and description, those two fields carry the entire weight of explaining what Agent B can do. A vague name like handle_it tells Agent A almost nothing useful.
3. A Capability, Not a Database Row

A tool exposed by Agent B usually represents a capability that requires judgment, not a simple lookup. Delegating a subtask means asking Agent B to reason about it, not asking it to fetch a stored value.
This is the core shift, the tool name describes a capability like draft_response_plan or review_pull_request, not a table name or a stored field.

code.content:
# Agent B exposes this tool over its own MCP server
@mcp.tool()
def draft_response_plan(customer_message: str, account_history: str) -> str:
    """Given a customer message and their account history, reason about
    the best response plan and return it as structured text."""
    plan = agent_b_reasoning_loop(customer_message, account_history)
    return plan

blocks.text: Agent A calls draft_response_plan the same way it would call any tool. What happens after the call arrives, an entire reasoning loop inside Agent B, is invisible from the outside.
4. How This Differs From Calling a Plain Tool
A plain tool, like get_weather or read_file, does the same fixed thing every time it runs given the same input. It has no memory of past calls and no opinion about what to do next.

Agent B, behind its tool, may reason differently each time, remember earlier turns in this exchange, or even decide to call other tools of its own before answering. The tool call looks identical on the wire, but what runs behind it is a whole second agent, not a fixed function.

items: A plain tool like get_weather always returns the same shape of answer for the same city.
Agent B, asked to draft_response_plan, might phrase two answers differently even for near-identical inputs.
A plain tool never calls other tools on its own, Agent B might call several before replying.

blocks.text: 5. How This Differs From Calling a Database

Calling a database returns whatever rows match the query, nothing more and nothing less. The database never changes its answer based on how the question was phrased, and it never asks a clarifying question back.

Agent B can behave very differently. It might return a partial answer, ask Agent A for more context, or take longer on a hard case than an easy one. Agent A has to be ready for a response that is not just data, it is the output of another agent's judgment.
This is why Agent A's calling code usually needs a bit more patience and a bit more error handling around an agent-backed tool than it does around a database call.

blocks.text: 6. Message Framing for Agent to Agent Exchanges

Message framing just means agreeing on the shape of what gets sent back and forth, so both sides can parse it reliably. For agent to agent calls, the tool call arguments and the tool result are the frame.
A well-framed delegation request usually separates the actual task from any context Agent B needs to do it well, rather than mashing both into one loose string.
Keeping the frame small and structured also makes it much easier to log, replay, and debug a failed exchange later, since every field has a clear meaning.
7. Structuring the Delegation Request
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441164194-933112451.png
A clear delegation request names the task plainly, includes only the context Agent B actually needs, and avoids assuming Agent B remembers anything from outside this call.

items: A short, direct description of what is being asked for.
Only the context needed to complete that specific task.
A correlation id so the exchange can be tracked end to end.
Any constraint that matters, like a deadline or a required format.

blocks.text: Notice the call itself is a single, ordinary tool invocation, all of the framing discipline lives in how the arguments are shaped, not in any special agent-to-agent syntax.
8. Structuring the Delegation Response
Agent B's response should be just as structured as the request. A plain wall of prose is harder for Agent A to parse than a small, predictable object.
Echoing the same correlation_id back is what lets Agent A match this response to the request it sent, especially once several delegations are in flight at once.

blocks.text: 9. Correlation IDs and Tracking a Multi-Step Exchange

blocks.alt: Correlation IDs and Tracking a Multi-Step Exchange
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441164195-960823282.png
Some delegated tasks need more than one round trip, Agent B might ask a follow-up question before it can finish. A shared correlation id ties every message in that exchange together.
Without it, Agent A has no clean way to tell which incoming reply belongs to which earlier request, especially if it delegated several tasks to Agent B around the same time.
The same id is also what makes a shared log readable later, filtering every message with req-901 in it reconstructs the whole exchange in order.
10. Coordination Challenges When Two Agents Decide at Once
Things get harder once two agents can both act on the same shared resource at nearly the same moment, each unaware the other is about to move too.
This is a genuinely different class of problem from anything covered so far, it is not about one exchange going wrong, it is about two independent exchanges colliding.

blocks.text: 11. Race Conditions Over Shared State
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441164195-978587375.png
Picture two agents both trying to book the last seat in a meeting. If both read "seat available" before either writes back "seat taken", both may proceed as though they succeeded.

This is not really an MCP problem, it is an ordinary race condition, made worse because the two callers are autonomous agents that may retry or act on stale information without a human noticing right away.

code.content:
# the unsafe version, read then write with no protection
if is_taken(slot_id) == False:      # both agents can pass this check
    mark_taken(slot_id, requested_by)   # both agents can reach this line

blocks.text: 12. Turn-Taking and Lightweight Locking
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441164195-761722541.png

The usual fix is the same one used anywhere else, the shared resource needs a single point that decides who goes first. Agent B's server can hold a simple lock per resource and reject or queue the second request.
The lock lives on Agent B's side because Agent B owns the resource. Agent A does not need to know a lock exists at all, it only sees the tool's answer.

blocks.title: Where the lock belongs
blocks.content: Put the lock next to whatever owns the resource, not inside either calling agent, since a calling agent can never see what the other caller is doing.

blocks.text: 13. Idempotency for Duplicate Delegated Calls
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441164195-982951970.png
Agents retry things, a timeout can make Agent A resend a request that Agent B actually already finished. Without care, that retry can cause the same booking or the same charge to happen twice.
Reusing the same correlation_id on a retry lets Agent B recognize the repeat and return the original result instead of redoing the action.

blocks.title: Idempotency in one line
blocks.content: The same request, sent twice, should produce the same effect once, not twice.

blocks.text: 14. Worked Example: Two Agents Booking a Meeting

Agent A is a scheduling assistant for one team, Agent C is a scheduling assistant for another team. Both need the same conference room at 3pm, and both talk to Agent B, which owns the room calendar as an MCP server.
Agent A sends a book_slot call with correlation_id req-901, Agent C sends one with req-902, arriving a few milliseconds apart. Agent B's lock lets req-901 through first and marks the room taken.

code.content:
# Agent B's server, handling both requests
result_a = book_slot("room-4-3pm", "agent-a")   # -> "booked"
result_c = book_slot("room-4-3pm", "agent-c")   # -> "already booked, choose another slot"

blocks.text: Agent C's own reasoning then decides what to do with that rejection, perhaps proposing a different room, rather than the lock itself making that call. The coordination problem was solved at Agent B, the response to it was handled at Agent C.
Notice how little Agent A and Agent C needed to know about each other, neither one is aware the other exists, they only know how to talk to Agent B.
15. Common Mistakes

items: Treating Agent B's tool like a pure function and assuming the same input always returns the exact same output.
Skipping a correlation id and then losing track of which reply answers which request once several are in flight.
Putting the shared lock on the caller's side instead of on the side that actually owns the resource.
Assuming a retried request is always a new action, and accidentally double booking or double charging.
Sending Agent B a huge blob of unrelated context instead of just what the specific task needs.

blocks.text: 16. Practice
Take a task you might delegate between two agents, like assigning a shared resource or splitting a report in half. Write out the request message and the response message as small JSON objects.
Then sketch what your lock or ordering rule would be if two agents asked for the same resource within a second of each other.
Finally, check your response message design against the table in section 8, does it give the caller enough to know whether the task truly finished.
Key Takeaway

An agent can expose itself as an MCP server just like any other tool provider, but what runs behind that tool is a second reasoning loop, not a fixed function or a database row, so its answers can vary and its calls deserve careful framing.

When two agents can act on the same resource at once, the fix is ordinary and familiar, a single owner, a lock, and idempotent handling of repeats, applied at whichever agent actually owns the shared state.
